szoveg_eredeti:
I knew things were a little off when the first thing I heard on my walk to the AI Music Awards was “the winner…” followed by the sweet voice of Kelly Clarkson.

No, Miss American Idol did not abandon her feud with the Brooklyn bird to capitalize on her newfound appreciation for AI. But as I approached the Mayan Theater in Downtown Los Angeles on a sunny afternoon to check in for Friday’s inaugural “AI Music Awards,” powered by the “Sonic Intelligence Academy” or “SIQA,” I wondered if her voice was so strong as to echo through the nearly century-old theater-turned-nightclub’s walls. To qualify for the awards, artists needed to register their tracks to SIQA’s “Verified Registry,” which denotes whether the song was fully AI-generated, made with the assistance of AI or featured a cloned human voice to lead the tune (what the group calls a “human + AI hybrid”).

Registered artists then nominate their peers in the 25 categories up for consideration — everything from “AI Song of the Year” to “Best AI Pop Song” to “Best AI Comedic Song” — and then vote on the winners. One of those nominees was Xania Monet, the AI persona of Telisha “Nikki” Jones, who a day earlier won the AI Album of the Year category at SIQA’s inaugural summit and who would eventually go on to win both artist and song of the year, three out of four of the awards’ top categories. (The fourth, producer of the year, went to “DJ Shawn Q.”) blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The Sonic Intelligence Academy is the brainchild of software engineer Timirah “TJ” James and her sister Mia James. Since its January launch, it has worked to establish an awards program to counter the mainstream music industry’s aversion to AI. The group believes there needs to be infrastructure that supports those using AI to create music, rather than dismissing its existence, and it hopes to be an AI counterpart to the longstanding Recording Academy that governs the Grammy Awards. It advocates for artists to publicly associate themselves with their AI-powered work, eager to highlight the humans who helped create the product.

It’s a noble, if surprising, decision to embrace its role as counterculture when AI artists continue to pursue a Billboard charting position. Some of its methods are a little overt, perhaps intentionally: After some in the industry spurned the idea of AI-generated music charting on Billboard’s industry-standard charts, the group used a week in January ahead of the Grammys to launch its own charts exclusively for AI music. The Mayan is a 12-minute walk from the Crypto.com Arena, the Grammys’ longtime home.

The moves are not subtle, but subtlety is not the organization’s goal. The group and awards’ existence alone reflects those in the AI music space trying to move past the thorny legal questions surrounding AI music, which have led to lawsuits by artists and record labels against generators like Suno and Udio over copyright infringement, and into a realm of relevance within the genres they’re trying to embody.

It is, in a word, new, and new things mean kinks to work out.

The first kink I noticed was when, as I arrived 30 minutes before the red carpet was set to begin, the doors to the venue were locked. I had to pull on each door before someone opened one, which led me to the check-in stand (bypassing any form of security, which didn’t seem to exist). I entered the foyer and arrived at the makeshift red carpet, where about 12, mostly independent media ventures set up cameras to interview the various nominees, presenters, and VIPs who’d grace the roughly 7-foot-long red carpet in front of one of the two step-and-repeat backdrops. A spokesperson told me 29 media outlets had signed up to cover the event, but that some couldn’t make it because of the sudden flight ground-stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration around 12:30 p.m. PT. The guests gracing the red carpet were not screens rolled out displaying AI avatars, contrary to a reasonable assumption. Instead, the human creators behind the digital faces strutted the carpet in their Sunday best, treating the night less as music’s biggest night and more as the biggest night for their music. Sequined dresses and colorful blazers strolled through, stopping to speak with outlets like Reuters to the fiery red mohawk-sporting, sequin-wearing host of “The Iconic Punk Oz” Oz Powers to, tucked against a wall and steps from the red carpet, an effective AI red carpet correspondent housed inside a tall, white faux-stone vessel. The contraption was developed by the event’s top sponsor, Deepgram, an AI startup specializing in text-to-speech agents.

The device, which knew the artists and pressed them about the event, struck in me a slight fear about whether people might opt for robot reporters instead of humans, though that fear subsided when I realized this device could not appear on the red carpet because it could not move. The creators seemed more eager to speak to the physical reporters anyway, with some of them emphasizing the human elements of their AI work. Fredro Starr, one half of the rap group Onyx, spent much of the carpet touting the human vocals that made up his AI-beat-laden record “It All Started in Brooklyn,” which he claimed was the first AI album on vinyl.

“You can’t replace [humans],” Starr told me, using the carpet to debut his new moniker, “Mad AI.” “The feeling that you get was what we bring with the spirit of hip-hop. So vocally, you can hear that, but the AI just took it to another level.”

Inside the theater, SIQA tried to bring a party-like feel to the function. A bar at the back of the venue —at a charge — kept well drinks flowing, and the bar top was littered with copies of a sponsored version of the newspaper “Rolling Out” featuring interviews with many of the nominees and James, the SIQA founder. One of those featured, Xania Monet founder Jones, sparked a wave of controversy last year when some of her Monet songs hit some of Billboard’s genre charts, leading to an interview with CBS’s Gayle King and to Kehlani slamming a $3 million record deal Jones received. cim: Megrendezték az első AI Music Awards díjátadót Los Angelesben
lead: A technikai bizonytalanságok ellenére a Sonic Intelligence Academy megrendezte a generatív zenének szentelt első nagyszabású díjátadót.
osszefoglalo:
A **Sonic Intelligence Academy** (SIQA) Los Angelesben tartotta meg az első **AI Music Awards** díjátadót, amelyet a hagyományos zeneipar mesterséges intelligenciával szembeni elutasítására válaszul hoztak létre. A szervezők célja egy olyan struktúra kiépítése, amely támogatja és elismeri az **AI-t használó alkotókat**. A nevezéshez az előadóknak regisztrálniuk kellett dalaikat a SIQA adatbázisába, megjelölve, hogy a zene teljesen AI-generált, hibrid vagy klónozott emberi hangot használ.

A rendezvényen 25 kategóriában adtak át díjakat, a főbb elismeréseket, köztük az **év előadója és az év dala** díját a Xania Monet nevű AI-persona mögött álló Telisha Jones nyerte el. A rendezvényt több szervezési és technikai fennakadás kísérte, a vendégek és alkotók személyesen vették át az elismeréseket.

A kezdeményezés a folyamatban lévő **szerzői jogi perek** és iparági viták ellenére próbál legitimációs platformot teremteni a generatív zenei műfajoknak.
miert_szamit: A zeneipari generatív AI-eszközök körüli **jogi és iparági elfogadottság** alakulása közvetlenül befolyásolja a szintetikus audio- és zenetartalmak üzleti felhasználhatóságát.
